newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communists demand sacking of powerful Kremlin aide.
newsitem.headline: Communists demand sacking of powerful Kremlin aide.

text.p: Russia's opposition communists urged Boris Yeltsin on Wednesday to sack his chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, stirring political tensions just days before the Kremlin leader is expected to undergo major heart surgery.

The call by the communist chairman of the lower house of parliament brought a sharp rebuff from the Kremlin, which accused him of interference and upsetting efforts to improve cooperation among Russia's political forces.

State Duma chairman Gennady Seleznyov said he could not work with Chubais, who led Russia's controversial privatisation programme from 1992-6 and then helped Yeltsin win a second term in the Kremlin in July before joining his administration.

"I insist on the immediate dismissal of the president's head of administration Anatoly Chubais. I do not doubt that I am expressing the opinion of an absolute majority of Russian citizens," he said in a statement.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov was quick to back Seleznyov, saying Chubais had acquired undue influence during Yeltsin's recent illness which was bad for Russia.

"We did not trust Chubais and his privatisation, we considered he did not deserve his (chief-of-staff) appointment and always said it would only worsen the situation in the country," Zyuganov told a news conference.
Seleznyov said he protested against Chubais because of the appointment on Tuesday of businessman Boris Berezovsky as deputy secretary of Yeltsin's policy-making Security Council.

Seleznyov said Chubais must have been behind Berezovsky's appointment to the influential organ, which he said was totally inappropriate. "If big bankers are going to get involved in the Security Council it should be called something different."
The leader of the liberal opposition Yabloko party Yavlinsky joined the condemnation. "Such appointments discredit presidential power and the authorities in general," he said.

But Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who has taken on more powers during Yeltsin's illness and will step in when he is on the operating table, said there was nothing wrong with Berezovsky's appointment: "I don't see anything bad in that."
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzembsky, referring to Berezovsky's academic credentials rather than his business interests, said parliament should mind its own business.
"The president's position is based on a strict observance of the Russian constitution and his adherence to the principle of separation of powers," Yastrzhembsky said in a statement.

"The protest of the State Duma chairman comes at the moment when thanks to efforts and initiatives of the president the country has seen a movement towards consolidation of different branches of power, their cooperation in the resolution of state problems," he added.
Seleznyov had been due to meet Chubais on Friday in a newly-formed consultative council, which is aimed at increasing cooperation between the executive and the legislature.

It consists of a "permanent four" -- Seleznyov, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, the chairman of the chairman of the Federation Council upper chamber Yegor Stroyev, and Chubais, standing in for Yeltsin.
Seleznyov said he would join the council only when Yeltsin recovered enough to take part in it himself, although Tass quoted government sources as saying it would go ahead anyway.
"Chubais is not a branch of power. I repeat, that I will work in the consultative council with pleasure when the president takes part." he said.

Berezovsky, 50, was assigned the post as part of a reorganisation of the Security Council following the sacking of its outspoken former secretary Alexander Lebed, ousted for his overt presidential ambitions.

A mathematician by training, Berezovsky has business interests ranging from car dealerships to television. He told Interfax news agency he was prepared to give up those interests if his new post required it.
